title: Learning Strategy: Teaching Students to Use Quizlet Effectively
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: In this practical, tools-focused post, Dave Stuart Jr. describes the two-step Quizlet routine he taught his students at the start of the school year for mastering essential unit knowledge such as terms, facts, people, concepts, and statistics. Students first take a Quizlet 'diagnostic' practice test to gauge their retrieval ability, then follow a branching protocol: those scoring 70% or better review missed items and retest to mastery, while those scoring lower first confirm they've had access to the material before using Quizlet's Learn function to build retrieval strength. Stuart reports that after explicitly teaching this process, including direct instruction via document-camera notes, his students' unit-test averages rose from 71% to 85% or better. He frames the results not as evidence of his own teaching talent but as confirmation that learning strategies act as multipliers of student effort when taught explicitly and practiced with 'no bells and no whistles.' The piece doubles as a mild rebuttal to reflexive objections to multiple-choice assessment, arguing the format is a red herring next to the deeper question of what effectively measures learning.
points: Stuart's two-step diagnostic-then-remediate loop (Quizlet practice test, then targeted review via Quizlet's Learn function, then retest) turns retrieval practice into a repeatable classroom routine rather than a one-off study tip.

Results are concrete: student average scores on knowledge assessments rose from 71% on the first unit to 85%+ on subsequent units after the strategy was explicitly taught and modeled via document-camera notes.
Stuart pushes back on reflexive anti-multiple-choice dogma, arguing the format itself isn't the problem; what matters is whether an assessment method effectively and sustainably measures learning.

The intervention requires no new technology or curriculum, only direct instruction in how to study smart; Stuart frames this as evidence that learning strategies act as effort multipliers, not talent substitutes.
quotes: We use Quizlet to organize the essential knowledge — such as terms, facts, people, concepts, and statistics — for each unit. The Quizlet is directly aligned to the knowledge recall assessments that our curriculum calls for.
I teach them what the word diagnostic means and why it makes sense here because we're going to use this practice test to "diagnose" our retrieval ability for key knowledge in this unit.

IF you scored less than 70% on your diagnostic, THEN first ask, "Was I absent during days where we learned any of these concepts? Did I miss any notes?" If so, get what you need to complete this learning.

For our first unit's knowledge assessment, my students averaged a 71%. During the second unit, I taught this process to students by sitting down at my document camera and having them take down the notes I was writing.
Nothing fancy — just straightforward, guided note-taking, direct instruction on how to effectively and efficiently move information into long-term memory and make that information easily retrievable.

My point is not that I am a great teacher. I promise you, I am just a good one like millions of others. My point is that the research is right: learning strategies act as multipliers of student effort.
